blocks.heading: Equations as amount relationships
blocks.text: A chemical equation communicates identities, states and reacting ratios. First write correct chemical formulae. Then change coefficients until every element has the same atom count on each side. Do not alter formula subscripts. Add state symbols when the substances' states are known: (s), (l), (g) and (aq), where aqueous means dissolved in water.

blocks.heading: Balancing with states
blocks.text: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide. The correct formulae are Mg, O2 and MgO. Oxygen is diatomic, so begin with Mg + O2 → MgO. Put 2 before MgO to give two oxygen atoms on the right, then 2 before Mg to restore magnesium balance: 2Mg(s) + O2(g) → 2MgO(s). The coefficients give the mole ratio 2:1:2.

blocks.heading: The stoichiometric route
blocks.text: For reacting-mass, gas-volume and solution calculations, use the same route. Convert the given quantity to moles. Use the balanced-equation coefficient ratio. Convert the resulting moles to the requested mass, gas volume, concentration or solution volume. Units are part of the data: mass uses molar mass, gas volume uses the molar volume at the stated temperature and pressure, and solution work uses c = n/V with V in dm³.

blocks.heading: Reacting masses
blocks.text: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g). The mole ratio CaCO3:CaO is 1:1. For 25.0 g CaCO3, n = 25.0 ÷ 100.1 = 0.24975 mol. Therefore n(CaO) = 0.24975 mol. With M(CaO) = 56.1 g mol⁻¹, mass = 0.24975 × 56.1 = 14.011... g, so 14.0 g to three significant figures. Rounding the intermediate amount to 0.250 mol happens to be close here, but retaining digits protects the final answer.

blocks.heading: Gas volumes at r.t.p. and s.t.p.
blocks.text: Methane burns as CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(l). At r.t.p., 0.350 mol CH4 needs 2 × 0.350 = 0.700 mol O2. Using 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ at r.t.p., V(O2) = 0.700 × 24.0 = 16.8 dm³. If the same amount were specified at s.t.p., the value would be 0.700 × 22.4 = 15.68 dm³. The condition named in the question selects the molar volume; it is not chosen from memory without checking.

blocks.heading: Solutions
blocks.text: A sodium hydroxide solution has concentration 0.150 mol dm⁻³ and volume 25.0 cm³. Convert the volume: 25.0 cm³ ÷ 1000 = 0.0250 dm³. Then n = cV = 0.150 × 0.0250 = 0.00375 mol. Conversely, if 0.00600 mol is present in 40.0 cm³, c = n/V = 0.00600 ÷ 0.0400 = 0.150 mol dm⁻³. Substituting a volume in cm³ directly would make the result 1000 times wrong.

blocks.heading: Limiting amounts and significant figures
blocks.text: When amounts of two reactants are supplied, compare moles divided by their equation coefficients. The smaller quotient identifies the reactant that runs out first and therefore limits the product. Carry extra digits through the calculation, then round the final answer to a precision justified by the data. State the unit and, for gases, the temperature and pressure. A bare number does not communicate the measured quantity.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Topic 1.4 replaces fixed molar-volume relationships with pV = nRT when pressure and temperature are supplied. Later inorganic and organic topics provide many reactions to which the same balancing and mole-ratio method applies.

blocks.heading: Consolidation and checks
blocks.text:
Take a mole ratio from a balanced equation. For N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g), one mole of nitrogen reacts with three moles of hydrogen and forms two moles of ammonia. If 0.400 mol N2 and 0.900 mol H2 are mixed, compare 0.400 ÷ 1 with 0.900 ÷ 3. The smaller value is 0.300 for hydrogen, so hydrogen limits the reaction and produces 2 × 0.300 = 0.600 mol NH3. Nitrogen is in excess.

Direct gas-volume ratios are valid when the gaseous quantities are compared at the same temperature and pressure. Otherwise convert each volume to moles using the temperature and pressure supplied. In solution work, distinguish concentration from amount: concentration describes moles per dm³, while amount is the actual number of moles in the chosen volume. Reporting c = 0.150 mol without dm⁻³ confuses the two quantities. At the end, read the question again: the requested substance, temperature and pressure, unit and significant figures belong to the answer.
